description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years) Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms. CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions. Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands

title.narrative: Greater and safer access to quality child protection and local SRHR information and services

comment.narrative: Child protection services, as health, psicological and counselling suport is included in this indicator - The survey findings revealed that 57% of social service workers are confident in their ability to manage and respond to cases of SEC, where 8% are somewhat confident, 31% are confident and the rest 18% are very confident in performing the tasks in various aspects of child protection, such as receiving referrals, conducting thorough assessments, providing support and documenting and reporting cases. This happens as they have a high level of education, and most of them work in public institutions in key or upper positions, where they feel confident to carry out actions related to prevention and protection of the SEC in the communities. On the other hand, 14% respondents’ need assistance, and 2% have no confidence to perform the tasks. The most significant findings under the indicator is that a significant proportion (20%) of the respondents don’t know their level of confidence as well as their responsibilities for performing different tasks related to handling and responding to cases of SEC. 7% of respondents did not want to respond to the question.
- Child protection services, as health, psicological and counselling suport is included in this indicator- Children aged from 8 to 18 years old

66 survivors were identified and 28 of them were rescued and had general diary in police station. They were referred by Upazila social welfare officer, law enforcement officials, court, local leader, local government, government officials and peer leaders. Once enrolled at shelter home, 28 survivors’ primary assessment conducted and based on their needs, they received shelter, food, cloth and attended issue-based session on life skill, gender, child protection, child sexual exploitation, early marriage, good touch bad touch, human trafficking, disaster risk, sexual reproductive health and rights. 28 survivors received health check-up and 16 of them received medical support. The health support was extended to survivors through private and government hospitals, offered sessions on personal hygiene, reproductive health, and unwanted pregnancy at the shelter. ACD team provided 16 group counselling, 52 individual counselling, 42 family counselling and 32 community counselling for reducing trauma and socialization process once they are back to community.

title.narrative: Children and youth access comprehensive correct SRHR and SEC information
# of young people (male) reached with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception

comment.narrative: Changed to Since we are looking at people reached with information given by SUFASEC during programme, we set this baseline value as zero

In the project area, especially children (below 18), adolescents (10-19) and young people (15-24) were initially unfamiliar with the term SEC/OSEC, and discussing such sensitive topics made them feel uncomfortable. Even, they are not aware of the various forms of sexual abuse and exploitation. Similarly, SRHR remained a taboo subject to them, and conversations about this issue were met with hesitation. They do not have comprehensive and correct information on gender and sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and parenthood, safe sex and contraception, consent and healthy sexual relationship, and engaging both boys and girls in discussions about these issues presented a significant challenge. They mostly do not know where to get information and services for the sexual and reproductive health. Moreover, adolescents and youth do not receive any program on SRHR or CSE in schools, no access to reliable information. In the school, the curriculum for SRHR or CSE is very inadequate or absent, and due to harsh gender and cultural norms, teachers do not like to discuss these issues with the children. Thus, it is difficult to reach children, adolescents and youth with SRHR or CSE, and inform on accessing support services.

250 children (boys 125, girls 125) are now united, they work together to prevents SEC within their community. Ten child groups, each consisting of 25 children, including those with disabilities, were formed with diverse selection criteria such as school-going, dropouts, working, differently-abled, indigenous/ethnic, and surviving children. These groups capacitated on child rights, child protection, life skills, and also contributing to child sexual exploitation prevention and survivors rescue efforts. All the group member received Standardized Adolescent Empowerment Package training focused on life skills, child protection, sex and gender education, health, technology, moral education, nutrition, pre-parenthood, livelihood skills, emergency response, and understanding human diversity and the role of children in stopping SEC.

Sexual exploitation of children both off line and online has been included.- Children in the age group of 12 to 18 are the target under the project.- The component of sexual exploitation of children is within the SRHR framework and linkages of SRHR particulary with OCSE and forced child marriage has been specifically considered.

In Year 2, adolescents and young people have received training in topics of SEC ,as peer-to-peer approach in their community they are now identifing SEC cases, and report and respond accordingly, and take initiative to receive them effective support services from the relevant service providers through referral and linkages process.
